title: Equal country weights raised the fitted coral heat slope in the Pacific sample from 2003 to 2010
abstract: We tested whether country survey weights change coral heat slopes. Four Atlantic and Pacific samples in 2003-2019 used 5,336 monthly units at repeated sites. Models controlled site, year, calendar month and depth. Equal country weights raised the early Pacific slope from 3.97 to 8.04 bleaching points per four TSA degree-heating weeks. The paired change was +4.07 points. Four-test intervals were +1.54 to +6.60 with country clusters and +1.82 to +6.32 with year clusters. The other three changes had intervals that included zero. Equal country then equal site weights gave an early Pacific change of +3.09, with a country-cluster interval of -0.07 to +6.26. Thus the primary result depended on the visit weight rule and did not repeat across all samples. Uneven coverage, sparse countries, missing reports, few clusters and one reporting system limit inference. The weights do not correct unknown reef selection probabilities. This is a survey-weight audit, not evidence of causal climate damage or species loss. Code, aggregate results, source hashes, checks and a figure are included.

display.caption: Left: fitted slopes on the same monthly records under three weight rules. Right: equal-country minus equal-month contrasts with separate country and year cluster intervals. Each interval uses four-test adjustment. Weighting changed the early Pacific slope, but the contrast did not repeat across all four samples.

citations.reason: Monthly frame and fixed-effect design inform this new paired weight audit. The raw data overlap; this is not independent data validation.
Prior split-response analysis on the same source; our outcome is total mean bleaching and our contrast changes survey weights.
